title: How Chili Peppers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore chili peppers: the name's origin (Columbus, Aztec/Triple Alliance usage), domestication in South America, the five domesticated species, capsaicin and pungency, the Scoville heat unit test (Wilbert Scoville, 1912) and modern liquid chromatography measurement, pepper classification by shape and heat profile, popular varieties (bell, poblano, habanero, Carolina Reaper, ghost pepper), pepper culture and competitive heat, buying, storing, and growing peppers, and health effects such as pain relief, endorphins, and cholesterol. The episode opens with banter about the Red Hot Chili Peppers band and closes with a listener shout-out.

segments.title: Opening banter and Red Hot Chili Peppers
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the Red Hot Chili Peppers being used at Guantanamo Bay, discuss the band's music and Anthony Kiedis's autobiography, then clarify they are talking about chili peppers.

segments.title: Name origin and domestication
segments.summary: The word chili came from the Aztecs/Triple Alliance; Columbus mislabeled the pepper as a relative of black pepper. Peppers were domesticated in South America about 6,000 years ago, birds disperse seeds, and there are five domesticated species in the nightshade family.

segments.title: Capsaicin, pungency and pain
segments.summary: Heat comes from capsaicin, concentrated in the placenta (membrane) rather than the seeds. Capsaicin triggers TRPV1 pain receptors and substance P, and topically it works as a local pain reliever. Fats like milk or sour cream dissolve it; peppers may also aid the stomach and thin blood.

segments.title: Endorphins and pepper eating
segments.summary: Peppers trigger endorphin release that can produce a high; humans appear to be the only mammals that purposefully eat peppers, which the hosts relate to the pepper's defensive burn.

segments.title: Scoville heat unit test
segments.summary: Pharmacist Wilbert Scoville devised the Scoville organoleptic test in 1912 to replace having people taste peppers, diluting extracts until heat is undetectable. Heat is still measured in Scoville heat units. Modern labs use liquid chromatography to measure capsaicin in parts per million, multiplied by sixteen to get Scoville units.

segments.title: Pepper types and heat profiles
segments.summary: Peppers are classified by shape, heat, and a five-part heat profile from the Chili Pepper Institute (heat level, onset, duration, location, flat versus sharp). Varieties discussed include bell peppers, poblanos, ancho, chipotle, habanero, Scotch bonnet, banana and pepperoncini, and paprika versus cayenne.

segments.title: Pepper culture and the hottest pepper
segments.summary: Chili pepper enthusiasts compete over heat, with no official governing body; Guinness recognizes a record. The Carolina Reaper, bred by Ed Currie, averages about 1,569,300 Scoville units; the ghost pepper held the title earlier, and Trinidad scorpion and Butch T peppers are also mentioned.

segments.title: Buying, handling, storing, growing, and health
segments.summary: Tips on choosing peppers, wearing gloves when handling hot peppers, storage and freezing, growing peppers from seed, and claimed health benefits such as lower cholesterol and blood pressure. A ghost pepper curry challenge in England is mentioned.

segments.title: Listener shout-out and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener shout-out to a sister leaving for college, followed by standard sign-off and contact info.
